titulo.texto: The Dining Room and the Tea Room

frase_gancho.texto: It is said that Maximilian ordered nearly five thousand pieces of silver for his table; here is what became of them.

puente_narrativo.texto: Move on to the Reading Room and the Games Room, where the palace set protocol aside to play and chat.

guion_corto.texto: Nearly five thousand pieces of silver, it is said, were ordered by Maximilian from the French house of Christofle to serve his table. The museum holds just over two hundred. Historian María Hernández Ramírez explains that the so-called Christofle silver is actually an alloy of nickel silver. In this dining room, according to the museum, that imperial silver is displayed alongside crystal glassware belonging to Porfirio Díaz. The fireplace and the sideboards, made of cedar, mahogany, metal, and marble, were built by Pedro Téllez Toledo on Díaz’s orders. The sculptor Epitacio Calvo decorated the room. Behind this room, according to the museum, a dumbwaiter lifted the food up from the basement kitchen. It is a table where the Empire and the Porfiriato share the same service. And the neighboring Tea Room changed its use five times: from employees’ quarters to the boudoir of Carmen Romero Rubio.

guion_largo.texto:
When people talk about Maximilian’s table, the first thing that catches the attention is the number. It is said that the emperor ordered from the house of Christofle, in France, a set of tableware of nearly five thousand pieces. The museum’s historian María Hernández Ramírez warns that it is not confirmed that all of them reached Mexico. The collection holds just over two hundred, with two monograms: the letters MIM beneath a crown, which stand for Maximiliano Emperador de México, and a crowned M surrounded by plant tendrils.

There is a surprising fact. The so-called Christofle silver is, in reality, an alloy of nickel silver. The researcher cites an analysis according to which silver made up only a minimal part of the surface. Its history in Mexico is also a long one: it was moved from the National Palace in eighteen seventy-nine and displayed at Chapultepec in nineteen forty-four.

The court’s cuisine was European, but made with local ingredients, according to an article in the Revista Bicentenario. At its head was the Hungarian Josef Tüdös, with a team of four cooks, two confectioners, six kitchen boys, a baker, and an inspector. At a gala dinner in Guanajuato, turtle soup, jellies from Morelia, and nougat from Saltillo were served. It was on the twenty-third of September, eighteen sixty-four. The menu was written in French. The same article notes that formal banquets were held mostly in the Imperial Palace, today the National Palace.

The dining room you see bears above all the stamp of the Porfiriato. According to the museum, the fireplace and the sideboards are made of cedar, mahogany, metal, and marble. They were built by Pedro Téllez Toledo on the orders of Porfirio Díaz, and the sculptor Epitacio Calvo decorated the room. The furniture bears the monogram of the Mexican Republic. The records cited by the museum list this space as the second astronomer’s room in eighteen seventy-seven. By eighteen eighty-two it already appears as a dining room. These are the same years as the observatory of the [Lions’ Staircase](chap_13_escalera_leones).

Behind the dining room, the work was enormous. The museum explains that a dumbwaiter and a staircase carried the food from the basement kitchen up to the anteroom, where dozens of servants worked. While toasts were raised at the table, downstairs everyone was running.

The Tea Room is dedicated to Carlota. The museum recalls that she received ladies from the most prominent families of Mexico and founded charitable institutions. When Maximilian traveled, she presided over councils and held audiences. As the situation worsened, she appealed to the European courts and to Pope Pius the Ninth, without success. Her story continues in [Carlota’s bedchamber](chap_18_recamara_carlota).

The information panel in this room includes a box about what this space was in other times, and the list is long. In eighteen sixty-six, under Maximilian, they were employees’ quarters. In eighteen seventy-seven it was the room of the director of the Astronomical Observatory. In eighteen eighty-two it was the bedchamber of President Manuel González. In nineteen oh six, the boudoir, or private sitting room, of Carmen Romero Rubio, the wife of Porfirio Díaz. And in nineteen thirty-two, a sitting room of President Abelardo Rodríguez. Rooms change their names with each era, and the current name is one way of telling their story.

One last scene from the imperial table. On the nineteenth of July, eighteen sixty-five, a banquet was held in honor of the Viscount of Sotomayor, envoy of the King of Portugal. According to the Revista Bicentenario, the highlights were artichokes in the Portuguese style, Berlin pudding, and quail pie in the Buenavista style. Silver from a deposed emperor and furniture from a president who governed for decades: that contrast is what this hall tells you today.

texto: Look for the monogram of the Mexican Republic on the furniture
Notice the materials of the fireplace and the sideboards, and tell the wood apart from the metal and the marble
If any pieces of Christofle silver are on view, look for the MIM monogram or the crowned M

texto.Fireplace and sideboards: Pedro Téllez Toledo, commissioned by Porfirio Díaz
texto.Service silver: Christofle (France), MIM and crowned M monograms
texto.Record of use: dining room in 1882, according to the MNH
texto.Key fact: Christofle silver is an alloy of nickel silver
texto.Tea Room, previous uses: 1866 employees’ quarters; 1877 room of the director of the Observatory; 1882 bedchamber; 1906 boudoir of Carmen Romero Rubio; 1932 sitting room

texto.pregunta: Myth: This dining room has been preserved just as Maximilian and Carlota knew it.
texto.respuesta: Reality: According to the National Museum of History, the fireplace and the sideboards were built by Pedro Téllez Toledo on the orders of Porfirio Díaz, and the room was decorated by the sculptor Epitacio Calvo; from the time of the Empire, the Christofle silver is on display.
